cards.statement: App Router layouts and pages are Server Components by default.
cards.explanation: Route-level UI starts in the server component graph until a client boundary is explicitly introduced.

cards.statement: The 'use client' boundary includes modules imported by the marked file.
cards.explanation: A file marked with use client brings its imported dependencies into the client module graph as well.

cards.statement: A Server Component passed as children can keep server execution inside a Client Component.
cards.explanation: The receiving Client Component places the supplied rendered output; it does not import or execute the Server Component implementation.

cards.statement: Date objects are supported props from a Server Component to a Client Component.
cards.explanation: React includes Date among the built-in types its server-to-client serialization supports.

cards.statement: Using server-only in a plain data module makes a Client Component import fail at build time.
cards.explanation: The server-only marker makes Next.js reject a regular client-graph import of that data module during the build.

cards.statement: An HTML details element rendered by a Server Component opens through built-in browser behavior.
cards.explanation: The browser implements the disclosure interaction for details, so a Server Component can provide that markup directly.

cards.statement: A Server Component can pass an ordinary onClick callback to a Client Component.
cards.explanation: A plain event-handler function is an unsupported prop at the server-to-client boundary; define that callback in client code.
cards.misconception: Ordinary event-handler closures can be serialized as client props.

cards.statement: A Server Component can read React context from a wrapping Client Component provider.
cards.explanation: Client context is consumed by Client Components. A provider surrounding Server Component output does not make that context readable during the server render.
cards.misconception: An enclosing client provider makes context available to Server Components.

cards.statement: Adding 'use server' to a component file declares its exports as Server Components.
cards.explanation: The use server directive identifies Server Functions. Server Components have no corresponding declaration directive.
cards.misconception: The use server directive is the component-level counterpart of use client.

cards.statement: A Server Component can pass a custom class instance as a prop to a Client Component.
cards.explanation: Instances of application-defined classes are outside React's supported server-to-client prop types, even when their fields look serializable.
cards.misconception: An object with simple fields is serializable regardless of its custom prototype.

cards.statement: A Server Component can manage a controlled input with useState.
cards.explanation: Interactive state managed with useState belongs in a Client Component rather than a Server Component.
cards.misconception: Server Components can retain local interactive state with useState.

cards.statement: An async function is a supported way to define a Client Component.
cards.explanation: React rejects async Client Component functions. Keep the Client Component function synchronous.
cards.misconception: The async component function pattern works in Client Components.

cards.statement: The RSC Payload is the HTML document that the browser displays during the initial page visit.
cards.explanation: The RSC Payload is serialized React tree data, a different representation from HTML markup.
cards.misconception: The RSC Payload and the HTML response are the same representation.

cards.statement: The RSC Payload includes references to the JavaScript files for Client Components.
cards.explanation: Where a Client Component should render, the payload holds a placeholder and a reference to its JavaScript file, which the browser then uses to hydrate it.

cards.statement: On a direct visit, Next.js renders Client Components to HTML on the server before hydration.
cards.explanation: Rendering on the server produces the first HTML, yet the component stays a Client Component: the same code also ships to the browser to hydrate that HTML.

cards.statement: On later client-side navigations, Next.js renders Client Components into HTML on the server.
cards.explanation: For client-side navigation, Client Components render in the browser instead of receiving newly server-rendered HTML.
cards.misconception: Client-side navigation repeats the initial server HTML pass for Client Components.

cards.statement: React uses an incoming RSC Payload to reconcile the active component tree.
cards.explanation: The payload is a serialized description of the UI. When a new one arrives, React reconciles the component tree and updates the DOM to match.

cards.statement: Hydration replaces the server-rendered DOM with a newly created page.
cards.explanation: Hydration connects React to the existing server-generated DOM and attaches the behavior needed for interaction.
cards.misconception: Hydration rebuilds the document instead of adopting the existing markup.

cards.statement: hydrateRoot expects the initial browser render to match the server-rendered content.
cards.explanation: The initial client result should agree with the existing server markup; hydration mismatches indicate bugs to fix.

cards.statement: suppressHydrationWarning can repair mismatched text during hydration.
cards.explanation: suppressHydrationWarning silences a mismatch warning; React does not repair the mismatched text as part of that hydration.
cards.misconception: Suppressing a hydration warning also corrects the differing text.

cards.statement: useEffect callbacks execute on the server while Next.js renders a page for its first browser visit.
cards.explanation: Effects execute on the client. Generating HTML on the server does not execute a component's useEffect callback.
cards.misconception: Server rendering runs Effects along with the component render function.

cards.statement: Shared layouts preserve their state during client-side navigation between their child routes.
cards.explanation: During navigation, the shared layout stays mounted while its child route content changes, preserving its state.

cards.statement: Next.js can fetch a destination's RSC Payload before the user navigates to that route.
cards.explanation: Next.js prefetches routes linked with <Link> as they enter the viewport: a static route in full, while a dynamic route is skipped or only partly prefetched.

cards.statement: On an initial render, reading a pending Promise with use activates the nearest Suspense fallback.
cards.explanation: use suspends the component while the Promise is pending, so the closest Suspense boundary above it shows its fallback until the Promise resolves and the content replaces it.

cards.statement: Nested Suspense boundaries let an outer section appear while deeper content is still loading.
cards.explanation: React streams the HTML of each boundary as it becomes ready, and later sends an inline script that swaps an inner fallback for its content once that content has loaded.

cards.statement: Components sharing one nearest Suspense boundary reveal together when their initial content is ready.
cards.explanation: By default the whole tree inside Suspense is one unit: if any part suspends, all of it shows the fallback, and then everything appears together.

cards.statement: Suspense can detect a fetch started inside useEffect and show its fallback while that request runs.
cards.explanation: A request started in an Effect does not itself activate Suspense; suspension requires a supported render-time resource.
cards.misconception: Any pending fetch automatically engages the surrounding Suspense boundary.

cards.statement: React preserves a component's state across a suspension that happens before its first mount.
cards.explanation: React retries a tree that suspended before its first mount from scratch, rather than retaining that unfinished render's state.
cards.misconception: A suspended initial render retains component state for the eventual mount.

cards.statement: A Transition replaces revealed content with a fallback when the same Suspense boundary suspends again.
cards.explanation: A Transition keeps already revealed content visible when its update suspends, rather than replacing it with a loading fallback.
cards.misconception: Transition updates hide already revealed content whenever new work suspends.

cards.statement: A streamed HTML shell includes the fallback of a Suspense boundary whose content is still pending.
cards.explanation: The shell is the part of the app outside any Suspense boundary. React sends a pending boundary's fallback HTML first, then the content with an inline script tag that replaces the fallback.

cards.statement: Sibling Suspense boundaries stream their completed content in component-tree order.
cards.explanation: Independent sibling Suspense boundaries can stream as their work finishes; source order does not prescribe completion order.
cards.misconception: An earlier sibling boundary has priority over a later boundary that is ready sooner.

cards.statement: Server-rendered page sections can arrive in chunks within the same HTTP response.
cards.explanation: The document response can remain open as the server sends additional rendered content.

cards.statement: Next.js can change the HTTP status code after a streamed response starts sending its body.
cards.explanation: Once the response body starts streaming, its status and headers are committed; later UI outcomes cannot rewrite that HTTP status.
cards.misconception: A later rendering result can replace the status of an in-progress HTTP response.

cards.statement: A segment's loading.js fallback can cover an await in that same segment's enclosing layout.
cards.explanation: The boundary created by loading.js sits inside its segment's layout, leaving that layout's own await outside the fallback's coverage.
cards.misconception: The segment loading boundary surrounds its own enclosing layout.

cards.statement: A shared layout stays interactive while loading.js displays feedback for the incoming route.
cards.explanation: During navigation, loading.js can show a loading view while the shared layout continues responding to interaction.

cards.statement: In the Pages Router, getStaticProps supplies props for build-time prerendering in production.
cards.explanation: The production build resolves getStaticProps before emitting the Pages Router page's initial static HTML.

cards.statement: In the Pages Router, getServerSideProps can use request-time data to render a page.
cards.explanation: getServerSideProps runs while Next.js handles a page request, so it can read request-specific inputs.

cards.statement: In the Pages Router, a nested UI component can export getStaticProps to load its own data.
cards.explanation: Next.js invokes getStaticProps as a page-level export, not as a loader exported by an arbitrary nested UI component.
cards.misconception: Each nested UI component can register its own getStaticProps loader.

cards.statement: In the Pages Router, getStaticPaths configures the paths for a page using getServerSideProps.
cards.explanation: getStaticPaths is paired with getStaticProps on a dynamic page, rather than with getServerSideProps.
cards.misconception: getStaticPaths configures dynamic paths for request-time getServerSideProps pages.

cards.statement: In the Pages Router, fallback: false returns a 404 for a path omitted from getStaticPaths.
cards.explanation: With getStaticPaths and fallback: false, Next.js serves 404 for paths outside the generated set.

cards.statement: In the Pages Router, fallback: 'blocking' shows a loading fallback while generating a new path.
cards.explanation: With fallback: 'blocking', the initial request for a new path waits for generated HTML instead of receiving a loading fallback.
cards.misconception: The blocking fallback mode displays a loading UI while a new path is generated.

cards.statement: In the Pages Router, App.getInitialProps preserves Automatic Static Optimization on otherwise eligible pages.
cards.explanation: A custom App using getInitialProps turns off automatic optimization for pages that would otherwise rely on it.
cards.misconception: Custom App data loading leaves automatic page optimization unchanged.

cards.statement: In the Pages Router, an automatically optimized page can receive query values in a post-hydration update.
cards.explanation: During prerendering the router's query object is empty, so on a dynamic route or a URL with query values, Next.js triggers another render after hydration to fill it in.

cards.statement: A dynamic URL segment forces request-time rendering.
cards.explanation: With Cache Components disabled, generateStaticParams can provide values that let Next.js prerender a dynamic URL segment.
cards.misconception: A dynamic URL pattern implies dynamic rendering rather than prerendering.
cards.volatilityNote: Rendering decisions are scoped to the previous caching model; Cache Components changes that model.

cards.statement: Reading cookies() in a page makes that page dynamic.
cards.explanation: In the previous model's automatic mode, cookies() needs incoming request data and opts the page into request-time rendering.
cards.appliesTo: Next.js 16 with cacheComponents: false and default route config
cards.volatilityNote: The route-wide effect applies to the previous model and depends on route configuration.

cards.statement: useSearchParams client-renders static UI above the nearest Suspense boundary.
cards.explanation: On a prerendered route, useSearchParams moves rendering to the client up to the nearest Suspense boundary; UI above it can stay prerendered.
cards.misconception: useSearchParams forces client rendering above the nearest enclosing Suspense boundary.
cards.volatilityNote: This prerendering rule is pinned to the previous caching model and the current hook contract.

cards.statement: Awaiting connection() in a Server Component excludes rendering below that call from prerendering.
cards.explanation: connection() waits for an incoming request before the subsequent rendering continues.

cards.statement: A Server Component can load its data by querying a database directly through a server-side database client.
cards.explanation: Server Components render on the server, so database credentials and query logic stay out of the client bundle.

cards.statement: Server Components making matching GET fetch calls can share a result during the same render.
cards.explanation: Next.js deduplicates GET fetch calls with matching URLs and options within the component render.

cards.statement: A data loader wrapped in React.cache can reuse its memoized result across separate server requests.
cards.explanation: React.cache memoization resets for each server request rather than persisting results between requests.
cards.misconception: React.cache provides persistent caching between requests.

cards.statement: Request memoization can deduplicate repeated GET fetch calls made inside a Route Handler.
cards.explanation: Route Handlers sit outside the React component tree, so its automatic fetch memoization does not apply.
cards.misconception: Component render memoization also covers Route Handler execution.

cards.statement: Server Components can share one React.cache-wrapped database loader to deduplicate matching queries.
cards.explanation: Reusing the same cache-wrapped database function lets its callers share results for matching arguments.

cards.statement: React.cache treats newly created object arguments with identical field values as the same cache key.
cards.explanation: Object arguments to React.cache must share the same reference to match; equal field values alone do not produce a cache hit.
cards.misconception: React.cache compares object arguments by their contents.

cards.statement: A fetch call made in the browser can configure Next.js server cache revalidation through next.revalidate.
cards.explanation: Next.js implements next.revalidate for server-side fetch calls, rather than as a browser fetch feature.
cards.misconception: The Next.js fetch extensions configure server caching from browser-side requests.

cards.statement: A page and its layouts can start their independent data fetching in parallel during route rendering.
cards.explanation: Next.js renders route segments in parallel, allowing separate page and layout loaders to begin independently.

cards.statement: SWR can use server-provided fallback data when its key matches the Client Component's useSWR key.
cards.explanation: The fallback only provides the hook's initial value. If the two keys drift apart, SWR ignores the fallback and fetches on the client.

cards.statement: React's use API lets a Client Component read a data Promise passed from a Server Component.
cards.explanation: Passing the Promise as a prop streams the data from server to client. Its resolved value must be serializable, and a Suspense boundary shows a fallback until it resolves.

cards.statement: By default, SWR treats server-provided fallback data as fresh enough to suppress revalidation after hydration.
cards.explanation: SWR considers fallback data stale by default and revalidates it on the client after hydration.
cards.misconception: Supplying fallback data automatically prevents SWR's initial client revalidation.

cards.statement: Upgrading from Next.js 14 to Next.js 15 preserves the default server fetch caching behavior.
cards.explanation: Next.js 15 changes server fetch requests to uncached by default, so an upgrade can require explicit cache configuration.
cards.misconception: The Next.js 14 server fetch caching defaults carry over unchanged into Next.js 15.

cards.statement: Server fetch calls can opt into caching with cache: 'force-cache'.
cards.explanation: Next.js then looks for a matching request in its server-side cache, matched on URL, method, headers and body. A fresh match is returned; a missing or stale one is fetched again and stored.
cards.volatilityNote: Scoped to the previous caching model.

cards.statement: A GET Route Handler can opt into caching with dynamic = 'force-static'.
cards.explanation: Route Handlers are not cached by default. A route config option such as force-static caches a GET handler, while other HTTP methods in the same file stay uncached.
cards.volatilityNote: Scoped to the previous caching model.

cards.statement: dynamic = 'force-dynamic' preserves persistent fetch caching.
cards.explanation: In the previous model, dynamic = 'force-dynamic' bypasses persistent fetch caching for the route.
cards.misconception: The force-dynamic setting preserves persistent fetch caching.
cards.volatilityNote: Scoped to the previous caching model.

cards.statement: dynamic = 'error' rejects request-time cookies() access.
cards.explanation: 'error' forces prerendering and caching of a layout or page, and fails with an error if any component uses a Request-time API such as cookies() or uncached data.
cards.volatilityNote: Scoped to the previous caching model.

cards.statement: dynamic = 'force-static' lets cookies() read incoming cookies.
cards.explanation: In the previous model, dynamic = 'force-static' makes cookies() return empty values.
cards.misconception: The force-static setting exposes incoming request cookies.
cards.volatilityNote: Scoped to the previous caching model.

cards.statement: fetchCache = 'default-cache' permits per-fetch overrides.
cards.explanation: With 'default-cache', fetch accepts any cache option, and a fetch that passes none is set to 'force-cache'.
cards.volatilityNote: Scoped to the previous caching model.

cards.statement: A route's default revalidation uses the lowest value in its layouts and page.
cards.explanation: Without Cache Components, the lowest revalidate across a route's layouts and page decides how often the whole route revalidates by default. A fetch with a lower next.revalidate can raise the frequency.
cards.volatilityNote: Scoped to the previous caching model.

cards.statement: The Client Cache retains its stored route payloads across a full page reload in the same browser tab.
cards.explanation: A full page reload clears the Client Cache; its previously stored route payloads do not survive the reload.
cards.misconception: The Client Cache persists across full page reloads.

cards.statement: Calling router.refresh() invalidates server-cached fetch results used by the current route.
cards.explanation: router.refresh() requests fresh rendering but leaves server data caches intact, so cached data can produce the same result.
cards.misconception: Refreshing the client route also invalidates its server data cache.

cards.statement: Back and forward navigation can reuse cached page segments.
cards.explanation: History navigation can restore cached page segments rather than rebuilding the destination from a new server response.
cards.volatilityNote: Client navigation caching policies may change.

cards.statement: Server fetch supports cache: 'no-store' with positive next.revalidate.
cards.explanation: Combining no-store with a positive next.revalidate is conflicting configuration; Next.js ignores both options.
cards.misconception: A fetch can simultaneously opt out of caching and configure a positive cached lifetime.
cards.volatilityNote: Scoped to the previous caching model.

cards.statement: Upgrading an application to Next.js 16 is enough to turn on Cache Components.
cards.explanation: Cache Components requires explicitly enabling cacheComponents in the Next.js configuration.
cards.misconception: Upgrading to Next.js 16 automatically enables Cache Components.
cards.volatilityNote: Cache Components enablement defaults may change.

cards.statement: An async component marked with 'use cache' has its rendered UI cached.
cards.explanation: Placing use cache in an async component caches its returned UI, rather than merely caching individual data requests.
cards.volatilityNote: Cache Components APIs may evolve.

cards.statement: Different product ID arguments give a 'use cache' function separate entries.
cards.explanation: A cached function's serialized arguments contribute to its cache key, separating results for different product IDs.
cards.volatilityNote: Cache Components APIs may evolve.

cards.statement: A 'use cache' function can read cookies() directly.
cards.explanation: Read request cookies outside the cached function, then pass the required values into it; direct cookies() access inside use cache is unsupported.
cards.misconception: A shared cached function can directly read the incoming request's cookies.
cards.volatilityNote: Cache Components APIs may evolve.

source.title: Cannot access request data in `use cache`

cards.statement: cacheLife accepts a custom named lifetime profile defined in next.config.
cards.explanation: Define a named profile in the cacheLife configuration object, then reuse that name in cacheLife calls.
cards.volatilityNote: Cache Components APIs may evolve.

cards.statement: A cacheLife entry past its expire limit serves stale data during regeneration.
cards.explanation: After the expire limit, the next request waits for fresh computation rather than receiving the expired cached value.
cards.misconception: Hard expiration continues serving the old value during a background refresh.
cards.volatilityNote: Cache Components APIs may evolve.

cards.statement: Assigning one cacheTag to two cached functions merges their results.
cards.explanation: A shared tag groups separate cache entries for invalidation; tagging entries does not merge their contents.
cards.misconception: A cache tag identifies one shared result rather than a group of entries.
cards.volatilityNote: Cache Components APIs may evolve.

cards.statement: A file-level 'use cache' also caches its named async function exports.
cards.explanation: The file-level directive applies to exported functions throughout that module, including named exports.
cards.volatilityNote: Cache Components APIs may evolve.

cards.statement: Passing dynamic children through a 'use cache' wrapper caches those children.
cards.explanation: Children passed through a cached wrapper as an opaque slot can remain dynamic; the wrapper does not cache their rendered content.
cards.misconception: Caching a wrapper also caches the dynamic children passed into its slot.
cards.volatilityNote: Cache Components APIs may evolve.

cards.statement: One page can combine build-time HTML with request-time personalized content.
cards.explanation: Partial Prerendering allows a build-time shell alongside personalized sections completed after a request arrives.
cards.volatilityNote: Cache Components APIs may evolve.

cards.statement: A short cacheLife expire can move cached content to request-time rendering.
cards.explanation: Very short expiration settings can exclude cached content from prerendering, even though it still uses use cache.
cards.volatilityNote: Prerendering eligibility depends on Cache Components lifetime rules.

cards.statement: A route's revalidate export remains supported for setting cache lifetimes.
cards.explanation: With Cache Components enabled, configure lifetimes through cacheLife instead of the unsupported route-level revalidate export.
cards.misconception: The previous model's route-level revalidate setting still controls Cache Components lifetimes.
cards.volatilityNote: Cache Components APIs may evolve.

cards.statement: A visit after the ISR interval elapses can trigger page regeneration.
cards.explanation: Time-based ISR starts regeneration when an expired page is requested, rather than running as an independent timer.
cards.volatilityNote: Scoped to the previous caching model.

cards.statement: Failed ISR regeneration discards the last successfully generated page.
cards.explanation: When ISR regeneration fails, Next.js continues serving the last successful page and retries regeneration on a later request.
cards.misconception: An unsuccessful regeneration removes the previously working cached page.
cards.volatilityNote: Scoped to the previous caching model.

cards.statement: A browser invokes a Server Action through an HTTP POST request when calling back to the Next.js server.
cards.explanation: Behind the scenes, actions use the POST method, and no other HTTP method can invoke them.

cards.statement: An authorization check in an admin page also protects that page's Server Actions from direct invocation.
cards.explanation: Server Actions need authorization checks in the action or its data access layer; a page-level check does not protect direct calls.
cards.misconception: Page authorization automatically applies to separately invoked Server Actions.

cards.statement: Calling bind on a Server Action gives it an extra argument such as the ID of the edited record.
cards.explanation: The bound value arrives as an argument before the submitted FormData. A hidden input could carry it too, but its value would be part of the rendered HTML, not encoded.

cards.statement: A Client Component can define a Server Action locally by placing 'use server' inside its nested async function.
cards.explanation: Define the Server Action in a server module marked use server, then import it into the Client Component instead of defining it there.
cards.misconception: An inline use server directive can create a Server Action inside a Client Component.

cards.statement: A Server Component form using a Server Action waits for client JavaScript to load before its submission can work.
cards.explanation: Server Component forms with Server Actions support submission before JavaScript loads or when JavaScript is disabled.
cards.misconception: Submitting a Server Component's action form requires loaded client JavaScript.

cards.statement: A Server Action can return its mutation result and the updated page UI together in the response to its invocation.
cards.explanation: When an action requests updated rendering, Next.js can include the resulting UI alongside the action's return value in one roundtrip.

cards.statement: Calling revalidatePath in a webhook Route Handler regenerates the page while that webhook request is executing.
cards.explanation: revalidatePath in a Route Handler marks the path for revalidation on its next visit rather than regenerating it during the handler call.
cards.misconception: A webhook's revalidatePath call eagerly regenerates the affected page before returning.

cards.statement: revalidateTag('posts', 'max') lets a subsequent read serve stale tagged data during background refresh.
cards.explanation: The max profile marks tagged data stale; a later read can receive the cached value while fresh data is fetched.
cards.volatilityNote: Profile-based tag revalidation semantics may evolve.

cards.statement: updateTag('posts') makes the next read of that tagged data wait for a fresh result.
cards.explanation: updateTag immediately expires matching entries, allowing a user to read newly written data rather than an older cached result.
cards.volatilityNote: The updateTag freshness contract may evolve.

cards.statement: A Route Handler can call updateTag to invalidate cached data after receiving a webhook.
cards.explanation: updateTag is restricted to Server Actions; invoking it in a Route Handler is unsupported.
cards.misconception: updateTag is supported inside webhook Route Handlers.
cards.volatilityNote: Supported updateTag call sites may evolve.
